top_cluster.headline: Following the January capture of Nicolás Maduro and the US seizure of Venezuelan oil operations, congressional Democrats are demanding transparency on where the oil revenue is going, amid reports that Trump-connected oil executives are already negotiating development deals with Venezuela's state oil company.
top_cluster.left_framing: Both outlets, from center-left to far-left, frame this as an accountability and self-dealing story: the Washington Post emphasizes congressional oversight and transparency about where seized oil revenue is going, while Mother Jones goes further, framing it explicitly as cronyism — Trump donors and allies personally enriching themselves from a war/intervention outcome, invoking themes of corruption and conflicts of interest.
top_cluster.center_framing: No center/centrist source is included in this set; the Washington Post here functions as the more institutional, oversight-focused left-leaning outlet rather than a true center source.
top_cluster.right_framing: No right-leaning source is included in this set, so right-of-center framing cannot be assessed from the provided coverage.

blindspot_narrative: The left is systematically avoiding the two campaign-trail character-attack stories (El-Sayed/Piker, Luria/ActBlue), leaving right-wing opposition research to run uncontested in the public record for now. The right is systematically avoiding the Venezuela oil cronyism allegation — a Trump-adjacent self-dealing story that, if roles were reversed, would likely draw aggressive conservative-media scrutiny — suggesting selective outrage calibrated to which party benefits rather than the underlying facts. Both sides continue to prefer symbolic Trump-personality storylines (Kennedy Center) over substantive legislative or financial accountability stories (Russia sanctions, Venezuela oil), which generate less follow-up pressure on either party.
